\subsection{Functional Time Series Forecasting: Canadian Weather Precipitation}
\label{subsec:cs3-fts}

The Canadian weather precipitation dataset records daily precipitation totals at
35 weather stations over a 365-day annual cycle, yielding a $365 \times 35$
data matrix.  We treat each station as a single functional observation — a
365-point daily precipitation curve — and stack them into a $35 \times 365$
array \texttt{Xfts}.  This casts the problem as functional time series (FTS)
forecasting \citep{hyndman_ullah_2007,hormann_kokoszka_2010}: the 35 stations
play the role of the time index, and the goal is to forecast the precipitation
profile for three additional (hypothetical) stations.

\paragraph{Decomposition.}
The FTS mean curve and principal components are extracted via
\texttt{fdars.fts.ftsm(Xfts, ARGd, ncomp=3)}, which fits the functional
principal component decomposition and a vector autoregressive (VAR) model on
the FPC scores.  Figure~\ref{fig:cs3-curves} displays the 35 observed station
precipitation profiles together with the FTS mean curve.

\paragraph{Forecasting.}
Three-step-ahead forecasting is performed by
\texttt{fdars.\allowbreak fts.\allowbreak ftsm\_forecast(Xfts, ARGd, h=3, ncomp=3)},
which accepts the raw data array and evaluation grid directly and returns a
\texttt{forecast} array of shape $(3, 365)$.
Figure~\ref{fig:cs3-forecast} shows the three forecast curves alongside the
observed mean precipitation profile.
The full analysis is reproduced exactly by \texttt{paper/code/casestudy3.py},
which writes both figures deterministically.

\paragraph{Honest caveat.}
With only 35 stations, the FTS time index is shallow: VAR estimation on 3 FPC
score series with 35 observations is illustrative rather than statistically
optimal.  The study demonstrates \texttt{fdars}' FTS interface on a real dataset
of the correct functional form; practitioners should interpret the forecast
curves as a software demonstration, not as a validated meteorological model.
